title: The Missing Box
author: The Last Analogue
summary: Using David Epstein's Inside the Box as a spine, this essay argues that humans do their best creative work when something pushes back, and that the constraints doing the real work are usually the involuntary, biological ones: mortality, fatigue, forgetting, scarcity of time. From Mendeleev's deadline to Bach's fugues, Oulipo's missing letter, and General Magic's fatal lack of limits, the piece shows that a constraint only helps when it costs something. It then argues that AI sits outside this box: its constraints (context windows, training regimes, RLHF) exist but cost the system nothing, so nothing downstream of its output is, for it, at stake. The human edge rests on answerability, being changed by, and responsible for, what one makes, and on the collaborative case where a human lends the machine their own scarcity through tight briefs and hard edits.
points: Creativity thrives under constraint: Mendeleev's periodic table came from a deadline, Bach's fugues from a rulebook, and General Magic collapsed precisely because unlimited resources dissolved its focus.
A constraint only does real work when it costs something; the involuntary limits (mortality, fatigue, forgetting, scarcity) are the ones that matter most.
AI is not free of constraints (training data, compute, RLHF, context windows), but those constraints cost it nothing, so they do not press on it the way a deadline presses on a person.
The human case for irreplaceability rests on answerability: being responsible for an interpretation and being changed by forming it, which AI output lacks.
The most interesting AI-assisted work comes from people who impose real constraints, tight briefs, hard edits, refusal to accept the first draft, lending the machine some of their own scarcity.
quotes: That’s the thesis of Epstein’s book in miniature: humans do their best work when something pushes back.
The distinction that matters here is not whether a constraint exists, but whether it costs something.

What’s easy to miss in Epstein’s argument is that the constraints doing the real work are usually biological. Humans forget, so they invent writing, then libraries, then search engines. Humans die, so they compress a lifetime of care into a single letter
It can imitate the form of a strange loop without living inside one. It can write a canon. Nothing about writing the canon changes the model afterward.
The gap is not the presence or absence of constraints. It is that AI’s constraints don’t cost it anything, so they don’t press on it the way a real deadline presses on a person.
The most interesting AI-assisted creative work right now comes from people who impose that kind of real constraint on the collaboration: tight briefs, hard edits, refusal to accept the first draft.
